# Introduction

When we think of a poisonous mushroom, what comes to mind first? Many assume that bright colors indicate toxicity, while others believe shape or form plays a key role. However, determining a mushroom’s toxicity requires analyzing multiple factors; making a mistake can be fatal. Mushrooms can vary in color, shape, and other attributes, but which traits are truly the best indicators of toxicity? What common misconceptions about these attributes exist?

In this project, we aim to answer these questions by training a classification algorithm using the UCI Mushroom Dataset, which categorizes mushrooms as poisonous or edible based on various physical attributes. Our primary goal is to minimize False Positives, as mistaking a poisonous mushroom for an edible one is far more dangerous than mistaking an edible mushroom for a poisonous one. However, we still want to be able to properly identify edible mushrooms, so we should still consider the True Positive Rate when evaluating the model. A low False Positive Rate ensures safety and the True Positive Rate becomes a secondary objective.

# Loading Data

```{r}
suppressMessages(library(readr))
suppressMessages(library(tidyverse))
suppressMessages(library(ISLR))
suppressMessages(library(glmnet))
suppressMessages(library(tree))
suppressMessages(library(maptree))
suppressMessages(library(randomForest))
suppressMessages(library(gbm))
suppressMessages(library(ROCR))
mushrooms <- read_csv("C:/Users/tommy/Desktop/homework/131/mushrooms.csv",show_col_types= FALSE)
colnames(mushrooms) <- c('class','cap_shape','cap_surface','cap_color','bruises','odor','gill_attachment','gill_spacing','gill_size','gill_color','stalk_shape','stalk_root','stalk_surface_above','stalk_surface_below','stalk_color_above','stalk_color_below','veil_type','veil_color','ring_number','ring_type','spore_print_color','population','habitat')

# Turning categorical variables into factors
mushrooms <- mushrooms %>% mutate(poisonous = as.factor(if_else(class=='p','Poisonous','Edible')))
mushrooms <- mushrooms %>% mutate_all(as.factor)

# Cleaning dataset, removing variables with missing values and removing odor
mushrooms <- subset(mushrooms, select=-c(veil_type,stalk_root,class,odor))
mushrooms <- na.omit(mushrooms)

# Splitting the dataset to about 80% train 20% test
set.seed(123)
train_ind <- sample(seq_len(nrow(mushrooms)),size=6500)
train <- mushrooms[train_ind,]
test <- mushrooms[-train_ind,]
```

# About the Dataset

The mushroom dataset is featured in UCI's Machine Learning repository. It features 22 categorical variables and the dependent variable is class, which determines whether the mushroom is poisonous or edible. The dataset has some missing values in the variable veil_type and stalk color, which we have removed from our models. 

# Model Selection

We decided to use decision trees and its variants to model our scenario. It made the most sense out of all the classification models, check the attribute of the unidentified mushroom and make a decision out of that attribute. We made multiple models using decision trees, boosting and random forests to see just how much information you really need to confidently classify a mushroom. We featured a model with all the variables, a model with just the variables related to the color of the mushroom, and a model with just the variables related to the shape of the mushroom.

## Disclaimer

The variable Odor, has a 99% accuracy prediction when it comes to poisonous/edible. Not only would this make for an uninteresting project, it would also not make too much sense in real life applications. Mushrooms can emit toxic fumes so smelling them might not be the best idea. As a result, the Odor variable has been omitted from all models. Additionally, note that spore print color is excluded from the color models. This is because spore prints are not related to the appearance of the mushroom and you have to press the mushroom onto a piece of paper to obtain the spore print color.

# The Models

## Basic Decision Tree


```{r}
library(rpart.plot)
suppressMessages(library(vip))

set.seed(123)
tree.mushroom <- rpart(poisonous ~., data=train)
prp(tree.mushroom)
mushroom.trees <- predict(tree.mushroom, type='class',newdata=test)
mushroomCM <- table(test$poisonous, mushroom.trees)

set.seed(123)
tree.mushroomColor <- rpart(poisonous ~ cap_color+gill_color+stalk_color_below+stalk_color_above+veil_color,data=train)
prp(tree.mushroomColor)
color.trees <- predict(tree.mushroomColor, type='class',newdata=test)
colorCM <- table(test$poisonous, color.trees)

set.seed(123)
tree.mushroomShape <- rpart(poisonous ~ cap_shape + stalk_shape + ring_type,data=train)
prp(tree.mushroomShape)
shape.trees <- predict(tree.mushroomShape, type='class', newdata=test)
shapeCM <- table(test$poisonous, shape.trees)
```

## Pruning

```{r}
plotcp(tree.mushroomColor)
optimalCP <- tree.mushroomColor$cptable[which.min(tree.mushroomColor$cptable[,'xerror']),'CP']
pruned_tree <- prune(tree.mushroomColor,optimalCP)
prp(pruned_tree)
```

As we can see, the pruned tree is exactly the same as the unpruned tree. This indicates that we do not have an issue with overfitting.

## Boosting

```{r}
set.seed(123)
boost.mushroom <-gbm(ifelse(poisonous=='Poisonous',1,0)~.,data=train,n.trees=1000,shrinkage=0.01,distribution='bernoulli')
summary(boost.mushroom)
mushroom.boost <- predict(boost.mushroom,type='response',newdata=test)
mushroom.boost <- ifelse(mushroom.boost >= 0.5, 'Poisonous','Edible')
boostCM <- table(test$poisonous,mushroom.boost)


set.seed(123)
boost.mushroomColor <- gbm(ifelse(poisonous=='Poisonous',1,0) ~cap_color+gill_color+stalk_color_below+stalk_color_above+veil_color, data=train,n.trees=1000,shrinkage=0.01,distribution='bernoulli')
summary(boost.mushroomColor)
mushroomColor.boost <- predict(boost.mushroomColor, type='response',newdata=test)
mushroomColor.boost <- ifelse(mushroomColor.boost >= 0.5, 'Poisonous','Edible')
boostColorCM <- table(test$poisonous,mushroomColor.boost)

set.seed(123)
boost.mushroomShape <- gbm(ifelse(poisonous=='Poisonous',1,0)~cap_shape + stalk_shape + ring_type,data=train,n.trees=1000,shrinkage=0.01,distribution='bernoulli')
summary(boost.mushroomShape)
mushroomShape.boost <- predict(boost.mushroomShape, type='response',newdata=test)
mushroomShape.boost <- ifelse(mushroomShape.boost >= 0.5, 'Poisonous','Edible')
boostShapeCM <- table(test$poisonous,mushroomShape.boost)
```

## Random Forest

```{r}
# Assign column names (as per the dataset documentation)
library(caret)

# Set seed for reproducibility
set.seed(123)

# Train a Random Forest model
rf_model <- randomForest(poisonous ~ ., data = train, ntree = 500, mtry = 3, importance = TRUE)

# Print model summary
print(rf_model)

# Make predictions on the test dataset
rf_predictions <- predict(rf_model, test)

# Evaluate the model using a confusion matrix
conf_matrix <- confusionMatrix(rf_predictions, test$poisonous)

# Print confusion matrix and accuracy
print(conf_matrix)

# Plot variable importance
varImpPlot(rf_model)
```

# Model Analysis

```{r}
suppressMessages(library(gridExtra))
mushroomImp <- vip::vip(tree.mushroom,num_features=10)
colorImp <- vip::vip(tree.mushroomColor,num_features=10)
shapeImp <- vip::vip(tree.mushroomShape,num_features=10)
boostMushroomImp <- vip::vip(boost.mushroom,num_features=10)
boostColorImp <- vip::vip(boost.mushroomColor,num_features=10)
boostShapeImp <- vip::vip(boost.mushroomShape,num_features=10)

grid.arrange(mushroomImp,colorImp,shapeImp,boostMushroomImp,boostColorImp,boostShapeImp,ncol=3)
```

## ROC and AUC

```{r}
suppressMessages(library(pROC))

pred_probs_tree_mushroom <- predict(tree.mushroom, test, type = "prob")[, 2]
roc_tree_mushroom <- roc(test$poisonous, pred_probs_tree_mushroom)
auc_tree_mushroom <- auc(roc_tree_mushroom)

pred_probs_tree_mushroomColor <- predict(tree.mushroomColor, test, type = "prob")[, 2]
roc_tree_mushroomColor <- roc(test$poisonous, pred_probs_tree_mushroomColor)
auc_tree_mushroomColor<- auc(roc_tree_mushroomColor)

pred_probs_tree_mushroomShape <- predict(tree.mushroomShape, test, type = "prob")[, 2]
roc_tree_mushroomShape <- roc(test$poisonous, pred_probs_tree_mushroomShape)
auc_tree_mushroomShape <- auc(roc_tree_mushroomShape)

pred_probs_boost_mushroom <- predict(boost.mushroom, test, type = "response")
roc_boost_mushroom <- roc(test$poisonous, pred_probs_boost_mushroom)
auc_boost_mushroom <- auc(roc_boost_mushroom)  

pred_probs_boost_mushroomColor <- predict(boost.mushroomColor, test, type = "response")
roc_boost_mushroomColor <- roc(test$poisonous, pred_probs_boost_mushroomColor)
auc_boost_mushroomColor <- auc(roc_boost_mushroomColor)

pred_probs_boost_mushroomShape <- predict(boost.mushroomShape, test, type = "response")
roc_boost_mushroomShape <- roc(test$poisonous, pred_probs_boost_mushroomShape)
auc_boost_mushroomShape <- auc(roc_boost_mushroomShape)

auc_results <- data.frame(
  Model = c("tree.mushroom", "tree.mushroomColor", "tree.mushroomShape",
            "boost.mushroom", "boost.mushroomColor", "boost.mushroomShape"),
  AUC = c(auc_tree_mushroom, auc_tree_mushroomColor, auc_tree_mushroomShape,
          auc_boost_mushroom, auc_boost_mushroomColor, auc_boost_mushroomShape)
)

print(auc_results)
plot(roc_tree_mushroom, col = "blue", lwd = 2, main = "ROC Curves for Models with AUC Values")

# Add the other ROC curves
lines(roc_tree_mushroomColor, col = "red", lwd = 2)
lines(roc_tree_mushroomShape, col = "green", lwd = 2)
lines(roc_boost_mushroom, col = "purple", lwd = 2)
lines(roc_boost_mushroomColor, col = "orange", lwd = 2)
lines(roc_boost_mushroomShape, col = "brown", lwd = 2)

# Add a legend with AUC values
legend("bottomright",
       legend = c(paste("tree.mushroom (AUC =", round(auc_tree_mushroom, 3), ")"),
                  paste("tree.mushroomColor (AUC =", round(auc_tree_mushroomColor, 3), ")"),
                  paste("tree.mushroomShape (AUC =", round(auc_tree_mushroomShape, 3), ")"),
                  paste("boost.mushroom (AUC =", round(auc_boost_mushroom, 3), ")"),
                  paste("boost.mushroomColor (AUC =", round(auc_boost_mushroomColor, 3), ")"),
                  paste("boost.mushroomShape (AUC =", round(auc_boost_mushroomShape, 3), ")")),
       col = c("blue", "red", "green", "purple", "orange", "brown"),
       lwd = 2)
```

## Model analysis for RF Model

```{r}
train_predictions <- predict(rf_model, train)
train_conf_matrix <- confusionMatrix(train_predictions, train$poisonous)
print(train_conf_matrix)  
test_predictions <- predict(rf_model, test)
test_conf_matrix <- confusionMatrix(test_predictions, test$poisonous)
print(test_conf_matrix)
```
We see that the training accuracy equals one. This indicates to me that there is overfitting in this model. The test accuracy is also one which indicates to me that the data set is easy to classify. 

```{r}
set.seed(123)

rf_model <- randomForest(poisonous ~ ., 
                         data = train, 
                         ntree = 50,   
                         mtry = 3,      
                         importance = TRUE, 
                         keep.inbag = TRUE) 

# Print model summary
print(rf_model)

# Extract and plot OOB error
plot(rf_model, main = "OOB Error vs. Number of Trees")

```
We can see as more trees are added past around 30-40 the error flattens to zero so adding more trees will not improve model accuracy. 

## Cross Validation for RF model

```{r}
set.seed(123)

cv_control <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

rf_cv_model <- train(
  poisonous ~ ., 
  data = mushrooms, 
  method = "rf",
  trControl = cv_control,
)

print(rf_cv_model)

cv_results <- rf_cv_model$resample
print(cv_results)

mean_acc <- mean(cv_results$Accuracy)
sd_acc <- sd(cv_results$Accuracy)

cat("Mean Accuracy:", mean_acc, "\n")
cat("Standard Deviation of Accuracy:", sd_acc, "\n")

```

# Results

```{r}
mushroomTPR <- mushroomCM[1]/(mushroomCM[1]+mushroomCM[2])
mushroomFPR <- mushroomCM[3]/(mushroomCM[3]+mushroomCM[4])
colorTPR <- colorCM[1]/(colorCM[1]+colorCM[2])
colorFPR <- colorCM[3]/(colorCM[3]+colorCM[4])
shapeTPR <- shapeCM[1]/(shapeCM[1]+shapeCM[2])
shapeFPR <- shapeCM[3]/(shapeCM[3]+shapeCM[4])
boostTPR <- boostCM[1]/(boostCM[1]+boostCM[2])
boostFPR <- boostCM[3]/(boostCM[3]+boostCM[4])
boostColorTPR <- boostColorCM[1]/(boostColorCM[1]+boostColorCM[2])
boostColorFPR <- boostColorCM[3]/(boostColorCM[3]+boostColorCM[4])
boostShapeTPR <- boostShapeCM[1]/(boostShapeCM[1]+boostShapeCM[2])
boostShapeFPR <- boostShapeCM[3]/(boostShapeCM[3]+boostShapeCM[4])

errordf <- data.frame(TPR=c(mushroomTPR,colorTPR,shapeTPR,boostTPR,boostColorTPR,boostShapeTPR),FPR=c(mushroomFPR,colorFPR,shapeFPR,boostFPR,boostColorFPR,boostShapeFPR),row.names=c('Mushroom','Color','Shape','Mushroom(Boost)','Color(Boost)','Shape(Boost)'))
library(knitr)
kable(errordf)
```


# Conclusion

From our model testing and results, we conclude that the decision tree is the best model for classifying mushroom toxicity, with a False Positive Rate of `r mushroomFPR`. We found that the random forest model  overfits the data so we looked at the next best model, which was the decision tree. The boosted decision tree, came close to the normal decision tree but fell short in the AUC/ROC test and FPR values. All in all, we found that a normal decision tree is better than both boosting and a random forest for this scenario. The random forest was overfitting the data and the normal decision tree had slightly better test results than the boosted tree. We also saw that pruning the decision tree did not have an impact at all, signifying that there isn't an overfitting issue.

Now back to the initial question. We found that while gill color is an important variable when classifying a mushroom's toxicity, it isn't as impactful as spore print color. Additionally, when we think of a mushroom's color, we think of the cap color, not the color of the gills. Thus, to answer the questions proposed in the introduction, the best indicators of toxicity are spore print color, gill color, and ring type. Contrary to popular belief, the color of the cap is not too important when it comes to determining if a mushroom is poisonous or not. Even in the model that utilized only color type variables, color cap came in fourth out of the five variables used in prediction. Next time when you see an unidentified mushroom, perhaps check the color of the spore prints, and not make a judgement based on solely the outer appearance of the mushroom.
